segments.desc: Patriotic nationalists who feel strong emotional and cultural bonds with fellow Guineans, viewing national identity as central to their sense of belonging.
Community-oriented citizens who agree they have ties with compatriots, though perhaps less intensely, seeing national connection as natural but not paramount.
Skeptics or those with weak national attachment who are uncertain about or disagree with strong national ties, possibly due to regional, ethnic, or class divisions.
Neutral respondents who neither strongly affirm nor deny ties with other Guineans, reflecting ambivalence about national solidarity.

Cautious citizens who feel constrained by social or political pressures; they experience self-censorship due to fear of criticism, harassment, or state reprisal, reflecting the pattern seen in responses about women facing harassment in public life.

Relatively confident voices who believe they can express themselves with reasonable freedom, though perhaps with some caution; they may live in less restrictive social circles or have greater education and resources.

Optimistic or politically engaged citizens who feel quite free to speak their minds, possibly because they are embedded in supportive communities or have not personally experienced serious consequences for speech.
Uncertain or disengaged respondents who lack clear experience with freedom of expression or prefer not to take a strong position on this sensitive political question.
Lower-income households without personal TV ownership, relying on community or family viewing; common in rural areas where electricity access is limited.
Middle-income urban and semi-urban residents who own televisions personally, valuing access to news and entertainment for their households.
Households where someone else owns the TV (extended family member or shared household arrangement), reflecting common living patterns in Sierra Leone.
A small segment with no response or uncertain ownership status due to ambiguity about what counts as ownership.
Skeptics of local government responsiveness who believe officials rarely listen to ordinary people, shaped by experiences of unresponsive bureaucracy and limited accountability mechanisms.
Optimists or those with positive local experiences who believe local council members often or always make efforts to listen, possibly from direct engagement or community involvement.
Uncertain respondents who lack sufficient information or experience with local government to form a clear opinion about council members' listening habits.
Skeptics of electoral integrity who believe the last election had significant problems or was not free and fair; influenced by concerns about presidential overreach seen in other questions.
Cautious optimists who acknowledge the election was generally free and fair but recognize minor issues; represent a moderate middle position.
Strong believers in electoral legitimacy who view the last election as completely free and fair; less concerned about institutional checks.
Disengaged or uncertain respondents who don't understand the question or lack sufficient information to judge electoral quality.
Rural and lower-income Mauritanians with limited healthcare access who frequently lack medicines or medical treatment due to poverty and weak health infrastructure.
Urban residents and those with better economic means who can generally afford medicines and medical treatment, experiencing deprivation only occasionally.
Vulnerable populations including the elderly, chronically ill, and those in remote areas who consistently struggle to access necessary medicines and medical care.
Those with strong social networks or access to NGO/international health programs who rarely or never face medicine shortages.

Democratic pluralists who value multi-party competition and reject authoritarian governance, consistent with their strong disapproval of military rule and support for parliamentary democracy despite current dissatisfaction with MPs.
Pragmatists open to alternative governance models who see single-party systems as potentially stable or efficient, similar to those who showed some acceptance of military rule.

Skeptical of fair distribution: People who believe local communities are systematically excluded from revenue benefits due to weak governance and corporate capture, reflecting the widespread distrust in government institutions shown in the first question.
Cautiously optimistic or uncertain: People who either believe revenue-sharing arrangements are adequate, haven't experienced extraction directly, or are unsure about the fairness of current systems.
Disengaged or non-committal: People who lack sufficient knowledge about extraction economics or prefer not to take a position on this complex issue.
Skeptics of government integrity who believe significant corruption occurred during pandemic response, viewing COVID funds as vulnerable to theft and mismanagement.
Moderate critics who acknowledge some corruption losses but believe the government exercised reasonable oversight, seeing the pandemic response as imperfect but not catastrophically corrupt.
Government supporters or those with limited information who trust that corruption was minimal or non-existent, believing most pandemic resources reached their intended purpose.
Uncertain respondents who lack sufficient knowledge about pandemic fund allocation to assess corruption levels.
Skeptical citizens who witnessed significant irregularities or have deep distrust of electoral institutions; they view the last election as fundamentally compromised with major problems.
Pragmatic moderates who acknowledge the election occurred but recognize it had notable flaws; they accept it as reasonably free and fair despite minor issues.
Optimistic or less politically engaged respondents who either lack detailed knowledge of electoral processes or prefer to view official elections positively; they see it as completely free and fair.
Uncertain or disengaged citizens who don't have enough information or understanding to evaluate the election's fairness.

Skeptics of local voice: Citizens who believe ordinary Kenyans have little to no say in natural resource extraction decisions, reflecting frustration with top-down governance and corporate interests dominating these processes.

Cautious optimists: Those who see some progress or believe communities do have meaningful input in extraction decisions, though they may be a minority or represent those with more positive experiences with local consultation.

Uncertain observers: Citizens without strong views on whether communities have a voice, either due to limited exposure to extraction issues or ambivalence about the effectiveness of any local input mechanisms.

Critical evaluators who view the government's pandemic response as inadequate, pointing to insufficient health facility resources and weak relief for vulnerable households despite some satisfaction with certain measures.
Cautiously optimistic citizens who acknowledge the government made reasonable efforts in health facility preparation and household support, seeing the response as fairly adequate given constraints.
Deeply dissatisfied respondents who see the pandemic response as emblematic of broader government failure, consistent with their very negative views on electricity provision and economic management.
Uncertain or disengaged citizens who lack sufficient information about the government's pandemic response to form a strong opinion.
Skeptics of police professionalism who believe police frequently disrespect citizens' rights, drawing on their observations of excessive force and lack of accountability in the country.
Cautious moderates who acknowledge that police sometimes operate professionally but have significant concerns about inconsistent respect for citizens' rights.
Optimists or those with limited direct experience who believe police generally operate professionally and respect rights, though acknowledging room for improvement.
Uncertain respondents who lack sufficient information or experience to assess police professionalism and prefer not to commit to a position.
Those who believe police rarely or never operate professionally, reflecting deep distrust in law enforcement institutions.
Pessimists experiencing economic hardship who see conditions as worse or much worse than a year ago, reflecting real struggles with cost of living and employment.
Cautious optimists or those perceiving stability who view conditions as the same or better, possibly benefiting from recent development projects or government initiatives.
Uncertain respondents who lack clear perspective on economic change or prefer not to answer, reflecting limited economic literacy or disengagement from national economic discourse.
Pessimists about government performance who believe crime reduction efforts are failing, consistent with their negative views on economy and electricity management
Cautious optimists who see some government effort in crime reduction despite broader dissatisfaction with other policy areas
Those with limited information or uncertainty about crime trends and government effectiveness in this specific area
Engaged citizens who participated in the last national election, reflecting active civic participation and interest in democratic processes.
Young people who were below voting age during the last national election and are now becoming eligible voters.
Citizens with uncertain memory of their voting participation or who chose not to vote in the last election.
Satisfied constituents who believe their local councillor is performing adequately and delivering services to their community.
Disengaged citizens who haven't heard enough about their local councillor's performance to form an opinion, reflecting limited visibility of local government work.
Critical voters who disapprove of their councillor's performance, citing corruption, lack of responsiveness, or failure to address local needs.
Strong supporters who strongly approve of their councillor's work and see them as effective advocates for their constituency.
Skeptics of government transparency who doubt schools will share budget information; drawn from those who distrust public institutions generally
Cautiously optimistic citizens who believe schools are more accessible and responsive than other government offices, willing to try contacting them
Uncertain respondents who haven't had direct experience with school budget inquiries and lack confidence in either direction
Socially engaged community members who regularly discuss current events and politics with family and friends as part of normal social interaction.
Occasional political discussants who bring up political matters sometimes when relevant issues arise or in specific social contexts.
Politically disengaged individuals who rarely or never discuss politics in social settings, preferring to focus on other topics or avoiding political conversation.
Skeptical of opposition parties; view them with distrust similar to how they view government institutions and current leadership. Believe opposition offers little meaningful alternative.
Cautiously open to opposition parties as a potential check on power; see them as somewhat trustworthy but not fully confident in their capacity or intentions.
Moderately trusting of opposition parties as legitimate democratic actors and necessary counterbalance to government; believe they represent real alternatives.
Highly engaged but uncertain; haven't heard enough about opposition parties to form a clear opinion, reflecting limited political information or engagement.
Urban and peri-urban residents who directly experience trash accumulation, poor sanitation, and water quality issues in their daily lives and view pollution as a serious community problem.
Rural or less-affected residents who acknowledge pollution exists but see it as a somewhat serious rather than very serious issue, or who are less exposed to visible pollution problems.
Skeptics or those with limited awareness who don't perceive pollution as a serious problem in their immediate community, or who lack knowledge about environmental issues.
Democratic accountability advocates who believe opposition parties have a crucial role in monitoring and criticizing government to ensure accountability and prevent abuse of power.
National unity prioritizers who value social cohesion and believe opposition should cooperate with government after elections to focus on development rather than partisan conflict.
Pragmatists and fence-sitters who see merit in both positions or are uncertain about the proper balance between accountability and cooperation.

Skeptical citizens with low institutional trust who distrust the President due to concerns about government performance (especially on basic services like electricity) and perceived corruption among leaders
Cautiously optimistic supporters who have some trust in the President, viewing him as a legitimate authority figure despite acknowledged governance challenges
Disengaged or uncertain respondents who haven't heard enough about the President or lack strong opinions, reflecting limited political information or interest
Dissatisfied critics who see widespread government failure across multiple domains (economy, relief, services) and believe electricity provision is being handled very or fairly badly
Cautiously optimistic citizens who acknowledge some government efforts in electricity supply and rate performance as fairly well, despite concerns in other areas
Uncertain or uninformed respondents who haven't followed electricity policy closely enough to form a clear opinion
Parents and community members who view physical discipline as a normal, accepted part of child-rearing in Tanzanian culture and see it occurring frequently in their neighborhoods.
Educators, health workers, and younger adults who recognize physical discipline happens but are increasingly aware of child welfare concerns and see it as somewhat frequent rather than very frequent.
Child protection advocates and urban residents who believe physical discipline is not very common or is declining due to awareness campaigns and modern parenting approaches.
Respondents uncertain about the prevalence in their community or unwilling to characterize the frequency of discipline practices they may practice themselves.
Strict literalists who require explicit confirmation in the context. They note that while boys are conversing, laughing is not mentioned, so they cannot confirm it's definitely correct.
Inference-makers who believe that conversations between young boys commonly involve laughter and amusement, so they see the statement as likely correct.
Skeptics who view the statement as definitely incorrect because the context explicitly describes conversation without mentioning laughter, treating absence of mention as negation.

Strict literalists who focus on what can be definitively proven from the context. They note the context explicitly mentions 'the man and the lady' (2 people) plus John McCain (1 person), totaling 3 people, not 5, making the statement definitely incorrect.

Flexible interpreters who consider that 'John McCain' might refer to multiple people or that there could be unstated additional people in the meeting scene, viewing the statement as neither definitely correct nor incorrect.
Charitable readers who see potential ambiguity in whether the context fully describes everyone present, leaning toward the middle category when exact counts are uncertain.
Literalists who focus on direct causation: They choose Hypothesis-2 because laughing is a more direct and immediate cause of realizing the zipper is open than merely being stared at.

Nuance-seekers who consider subtle social cues: They choose Hypothesis-1 because noticing stares is a more plausible intermediate step that would lead someone to check their appearance and discover the problem.
Literal interpreters who recognize that the statement 'A person sitting' is factually supported by the context describing a woman sitting at a desk, making this definitely correct.
Cautious skeptics who worry about unstated details or want more specificity about which person or exact circumstances, leading them to choose the middle option despite clear evidence.

Literal interpreters who recognize that the statement directly paraphrases the context with clear logical correspondence between 'He walked out into the street and I followed' and 'I followed him down the street.'

Cautious skeptics who note minor semantic differences (the context doesn't explicitly say 'down the street' or confirm the speaker followed him specifically down it rather than just out into it) and prefer to hedge with option C.
Literalists who recognize that a hand flute is a specific type of instrument, making the statement a valid generalization that is definitely correct.

Skeptics who question whether the level of specificity matters or worry about unstated assumptions, viewing the relationship between 'hand flute' and 'instrument' as ambiguous enough to warrant the middle category.

Logical causality reasoners who select hypotheses that directly explain the negative outcome. They recognize that an allergic reaction (Hypothesis-1) is the most plausible cause of vomiting, making it the clear answer.

Optimistic or alternative-focused thinkers who prefer Hypothesis-2 because they focus on the positive experience of trying new flavors, or who may not make the allergic reaction connection as readily.

Literal interpreters who focus on what can be definitively confirmed from the context. They note that while different jerseys suggest opposing teams, the context only explicitly states the players are 'at the starting line' and doesn't confirm they are actually from opposing teams or that a 'face off' is occurring.

Pragmatic reasoners who infer from context clues. They see different colored jerseys (orange vs white) as strong evidence of opposing teams and interpret 'set at the starting line' as a face-off situation, making the statement definitely or likely correct.

Skeptics who reject the statement as definitely incorrect, either because 'face off' implies direct confrontation not clearly shown, or because the context doesn't explicitly state these are opposing teams despite the jersey colors.

Causal chain thinkers who prioritize narrative coherence: they favor hypotheses that explain how the beginning state logically leads to the ending through a clear cause-and-effect sequence. They recognize that Hypothesis-2 (injury + affordability issue) directly enables the ending (getting a brace), making it the more plausible causal bridge.

Literalists who focus on explicit textual connections: they notice that Hypothesis-1 introduces a broken leg but doesn't clearly connect to why a brace would help, while Hypothesis-2 directly mentions a brace, making the ending feel more directly connected to this hypothesis regardless of narrative logic.

Pragmatic reasoners who focus on plausibility and causal logic: they recognize that finding a cat in the garden is a more straightforward and realistic path to the ending than begging for a feral cat, which introduces unnecessary complications.
Literalists who interpret 'begged for a feral cat' as a valid causal path and don't penalize it for being less conventional or practical than finding a cat.

Strict literalists who focus on direct contradictions between context and statement. The context says 'sitting on a chair on the sidewalk playing an instrument' while the statement says 'dancing in the park' - these are factually incompatible on multiple dimensions (activity, location, posture).

Charitable interpreters who see potential ambiguity or indirect connections. They might consider that street musicians could be moving rhythmically, or that 'dancing' and 'playing music' could be loosely related activities, making the answer less clear-cut.

Literal interpreters who focus on the exact words spoken. The context says 'thanks bye bye' which doesn't explicitly contain 'that's great see you later,' so they see this as neither definitely correct nor incorrect—the sentiment aligns but the words don't match.
Strict literalists who view this as definitely incorrect because the statement uses completely different words and phrases than what was actually said in the context.
Pragmatic interpreters who see the statements as functionally equivalent—both are polite closings expressing satisfaction and farewell—making it definitely correct despite different wording.

Literal connectors who focus on specific details: They notice that Hypothesis-2 explicitly mentions 'at the park' and 'at lunch,' which directly matches the O-Ending's 'park in a secluded spot,' making it the more plausible causal link.

Holistic reasoners who prioritize broader context: They see Hypothesis-1 as more relevant because practicing yoga 'late at night' in a secluded spot makes more logical sense for privacy and safety reasons, even though it's less explicitly matched to the ending.

Literal causality reasoners who focus on which hypothesis directly explains the O-Ending outcome. They recognize that Tom's jealousy/suspicion (Hypothesis-1) directly causes the argument escalation and his demand for Ana to leave, making it the clear causal link.

Alternative explanation seekers who consider that Ana's innocent explanation (Hypothesis-2) could still lead to the ending if Tom irrationally rejects it or if there are other unstated factors, preferring to keep multiple interpretations open.

Literalists who focus on the exact wording: the statement says townsfolk 'think' it sounds convincing, while the context only reports what it sounds like 'in their mouths,' which doesn't explicitly confirm their internal thoughts. They choose (C) because the inference requires assumption.

Pragmatic readers who interpret 'in the mouths of' as a natural expression indicating what people are actually saying/thinking, treating the statement as a reasonable inference from context. They choose (A).
Cautious interpreters who recognize the statement could be correct but see enough ambiguity in the phrasing to warrant (C) as the safest answer, avoiding overconfidence in inference.
Pragmatists who recognize that repeatedly doing surveys without winning is a waste of time, and that Pam's lack of concern suggests she's rationalizing unproductive behavior.
Optimists who believe Pam's honesty and genuine effort in the surveys is what matters, and that her contentment reflects a positive attitude regardless of outcomes.
Strict literalists who notice the phone number changed from (202) to (555) and mark this as definitely incorrect factual information.

Charitable interpreters who see this as a minor transcription error or assume the statement is attempting to convey the general idea despite the number discrepancy, choosing neither correct nor incorrect.

Logical reasoners who evaluate causal plausibility: They recognize that Hypothesis-2 (deciding to look at boats while grocery shopping) is a more direct and plausible causal pathway to buying a yacht than Hypothesis-1 (seeing a car advertisement), even though both are somewhat absurd. They pick B.

Literalists or contrarians who focus on the absurdity of the scenario: They may pick A because they view both hypotheses as equally implausible, or they reject the premise that either hypothesis reasonably leads to yacht purchase. They pick A.

Strict literalists who focus on direct contradictions between context and statement. They notice the context mentions one woman and a bicycle, while the statement claims three people riding bicycles, making it definitely incorrect.

Charitable interpreters who see potential ambiguity or acknowledge they lack complete information about the scene, so they hedge toward 'neither definitely correct nor incorrect' despite the apparent contradiction.
Careful readers who note the context explicitly states turquoise (not gold) as the source, making the statement factually incorrect based on the given information.

Uncertain reasoners who recognize the statement contradicts the context but wonder if additional historical knowledge about Egyptian gold mining might make it partially true, so they hedge toward option C.
Literal interpreters who focus on the word 'source' and may conflate different Egyptian resources or assume the statement could be correct despite the context, choosing option A.
Logical reasoners who recognize that sexual abuse and mental abuse are distinct phenomena, so the statement makes an unsupported leap from the context; they pick (B) definitely incorrect.

Holistic thinkers who see the statement as a reasonable inference since sexual abuse often causes mental abuse, or who interpret it charitably as related to the abuse topic; they pick (A) definitely correct.

Cautious interpreters who note that while mental abuse may exist and be related to the context, the statement introduces new information not explicitly stated, making it neither provably correct nor incorrect; they pick (C) neither.
Literal interpreters who recognize that the context explicitly states the man is 'taking a picture' with a camera, making the statement directly supported and definitely correct.

Cautious skeptics who note that while 'taking a picture' strongly implies camera use, they want explicit mention of the word 'camera' before marking it definitely correct, choosing the middle option instead.

Pragmatic reasoners who focus on what actually causes the outcome: they recognize that screeching while pointing to the tummy signals hunger/need, which directly motivates the child to feed the monkey, making Hypothesis-2 the clear causal link.

Literalists who interpret 'scared the kids away' as incompatible with kids staying to feed the monkey, but struggle with the typo ('money' vs 'monkey') and may give Hypothesis-1 credit for being a plausible intermediate event despite not leading to the ending.
Literal interpreters who recognize that a foul shot IS an extra shot from the line, making the statement definitely correct despite the typo ('fro' for 'from').

Strict graders who view the statement as ambiguous or incorrect due to the spelling error 'fro' instead of 'from', or who interpret 'extra shots' as implying multiple shots beyond the standard foul attempt.
Literal interpreters who recognize that 'shot the other' directly contradicts 'kept his gun holstered,' making the statement definitely incorrect.

Ambiguity-focused respondents who consider alternative interpretations (e.g., 'shot' could mean something other than firing a gun, or the holstering could have happened at a different time) and select the middle option.

Risk-averse investors who strongly prefer certainty and guaranteed returns, especially when the certain option has a meaningful advantage. They view the $3.4 difference as significant enough to justify avoiding the lottery.

Expected value maximizers and risk-tolerant gamblers who focus on the mathematical distribution and are willing to accept lower expected value for the chance at higher outcomes, or who underweight the certainty premium.
Expected value maximizers who strongly prefer certainty when it's positive and avoid likely losses. They recognize A is clearly superior here.
Risk-seeking gamblers or those who occasionally misread probabilities, willing to take the small chance at positive outcomes in B despite the 75% loss probability.
Expected Value Maximizers: Calculate the mathematical expected value and choose Machine B despite the 50% loss risk, as the $4.50 EV significantly exceeds Machine A's $3.0.

Risk-Averse Certainty Seekers: Strongly prefer Machine A's guaranteed $3.0 outcome over the 50% chance of losing $15, viewing the certain bonus as more valuable than higher expected value with downside risk.
Risk-averse maximizers who prefer guaranteed outcomes with good expected value, choosing the certain $19 over a 50/50 gamble with slightly higher expected value ($19 vs $19).

Expected value optimizers who recognize that Machine B has a marginally higher expected value ($19 vs $19) and are willing to accept small risks for potential gains, or who view the two options as essentially equivalent and choose the variable option.
Expected value maximizers who choose the option with higher mathematical expected value, especially when the difference is substantial.
Risk-averse individuals who prefer the more stable option with lower variance, even if expected value is slightly lower.
Expected value maximizers who also prefer lower variance when possible. They choose Machine A because it offers both higher EV and certainty.
Risk-seeking gamblers or those who miscalculate probabilities. They might prefer Machine B's upside potential despite lower EV.
Risk-averse decision makers who prefer certainty and simpler payoff structures, choosing Machine A for its clearer risk profile despite nearly identical expected values.
Expected value maximizers and risk-tolerant individuals who carefully calculate probabilities and are comfortable with the complexity of Machine B's distribution for marginally similar returns.
Expected value maximizers who choose the option with higher mathematical expected value, especially when gains are likely. They prioritize long-term optimization over safety.
Risk-averse individuals who prefer the safer option with high probability of positive outcome, even if it sacrifices expected value. They avoid the 60% chance of significant loss.
Expected value maximizers who calculate and choose the option with higher mathematical expectation, even when differences are small
Risk-averse decision-makers who prefer high-probability outcomes and certainty, choosing Machine A's 90% chance of $9 over the riskier Machine B
Expected value maximizers who calculate that Machine A's certain -$2 loss is better than Machine B's -$5 expected value, and choose rationally.
Loss aversion avoiders who prefer the 50% chance of a positive outcome (+$6) in Machine B over the guaranteed loss in Machine A, despite worse expected value.
Expected value maximizers who also prefer certainty when available. They recognize Machine A offers both higher expected value ($18 vs $12.75) and zero risk.
Risk-seeking or variance-preferring individuals who occasionally choose lower expected value options for the chance at different outcomes, or who misread the probabilities.
Expected value maximizers who do the math and pick the option with marginally higher EV, choosing B for its slightly superior expected value and more balanced risk distribution.
Certainty-seekers and loss-averse decision makers who prefer Machine A's higher probability of the $25 outcome, viewing the guaranteed $25 as more reliable than B's split distribution.
Expected value maximizers who calculate probabilities and choose the option with higher mathematical expected value, regardless of certainty
Certainty-seeking individuals who prefer guaranteed outcomes and are willing to accept lower expected value to avoid risk
Expected value maximizers who choose the option with the highest mathematical expected value, preferring Machine B's 99% chance at $11 plus 1% upside over the certain $9.
Certainty-preference individuals who strongly favor guaranteed outcomes and choose Machine A's certain $9 to avoid any risk, even when expected value is lower.
Expected value maximizers who consistently choose the option with higher mathematical expected value, especially when the difference is substantial.
Risk-averse decision makers who prefer options with higher probability of positive outcomes or smaller guaranteed losses, even when EV is lower.
Expected value maximizers who prefer certainty and low variance. They choose Machine A because it guarantees $30 with no risk, valuing the sure $3 bonus over uncertain outcomes.

Risk-tolerant expected value calculators who recognize that Machine B's expected value (~$20.50) is lower than Machine A's ($30), but are drawn to the possibility of higher payoffs and the variance in outcomes.
Expected value maximizers who calculate the math: Machine A has -$8 EV vs Machine B's -$17.9 EV, making the choice clear.
Loss-averse risk minimizers who strongly prefer the guaranteed -$6 loss over the 90% chance of -$21 loss, regardless of the small upside.
Variance seekers attracted to the 10% chance of $82 despite poor expected value and high downside risk.
Expected value maximizers who consistently choose higher mathematical payoffs, even with small probabilities of large gains
Risk-averse individuals who prefer guaranteed modest returns over uncertain outcomes, especially when the upside probability is very low (1%)
Expected value maximizers who calculate and choose the option with higher mathematical expected value, favoring Machine B's $28.00 EV advantage.
Risk-averse responders who prefer Machine A's more consistent payoffs ($19-29 range) over Machine B's higher variance despite similar expected values.
Upside-focused gamblers attracted to Machine B's $82 maximum payoff, willing to accept lower probability for the chance at a much larger reward.
Expected value maximizers who prefer certainty and avoid worse gambles. They calculate that Machine A's guaranteed -$7 loss is better than Machine B's expected -$11.45 loss.
Risk-seeking gamblers or those who misread the probabilities, hoping for the small chance of better outcomes in Machine B despite worse expected value.
Expected value maximizers who calculate probabilities and choose the option with highest EV, preferring B's $30.69 expected value despite the small downside risk.
Certainty and safety-focused decision makers who strongly prefer guaranteed outcomes and avoid tail risks, choosing A's certain $23 reward.
Expected value maximizers who choose the option with higher EV and lower risk. They recognize A's guaranteed $21 beats B's lower expected value with unnecessary variance.
Risk-seeking or variance-preferring individuals who occasionally choose the option with more variability despite lower expected value, or who miscalculate the probabilities.
Certainty-seekers who prefer guaranteed outcomes when alternatives offer minimal additional expected value and negligible upside potential.
Expected value maximizers who consistently choose the option with higher mathematical expected value, even when the difference is small and variance is low.
Expected value maximizers who consistently choose options with higher mathematical payoffs, even with some variance. They see this as a straightforward optimization problem.
Risk-averse individuals who prefer certainty and guaranteed outcomes, choosing the sure $10 over probabilistic alternatives regardless of expected value.

Skeptics of conspiracy theories who trust mainstream scientific and institutional accounts. They reject claims about deliberate creation and spread of diseases.
Conspiracy-minded individuals who believe powerful groups deliberately create and weaponize diseases for population control or other nefarious purposes.
Uncertain or agnostic respondents who lack strong conviction either way, reflecting general skepticism about what can be known about origins of major diseases.
Skeptics of hidden truths who apply critical thinking to extraordinary claims and trust mainstream scientific consensus on space exploration and contact scenarios.
Open-minded conspiracy theorists who believe governments systematically hide major discoveries from the public, seeing alien contact as plausible given patterns in other cover-ups.
Moderate doubters who think alien contact is unlikely but acknowledge the possibility that governments might conceal such information if it occurred.
Uncertain respondents who lack strong convictions about either alien existence or government transparency on this topic.
Skeptics of conspiracy theories who reject the idea of a secret world government, viewing it as unfounded speculation lacking credible evidence.
Moderate skeptics who think such claims are probably false but acknowledge some uncertainty about hidden power structures.
Conspiracy-minded individuals who believe there is likely a shadowy group controlling world events, reflecting broader distrust of official narratives.
Uncertain respondents who lack strong conviction either way and express genuine uncertainty about whether secret global control exists.

Skeptics of official narratives who distrust government and institutional claims, particularly regarding major historical events and scientific consensus. They tend to believe alternative explanations for significant events.
Pragmatic doubters who are uncertain about the moon landing but lean toward skepticism due to general distrust of authorities and limited personal verification of space achievements.
Science-minded individuals who accept the moon landing as real based on scientific evidence, documentation, and the implausibility of such a massive conspiracy remaining hidden.
Undecided or disengaged respondents who lack strong opinions on historical space events and may not have sufficient knowledge to form confident beliefs.
Skeptics of official narratives who distrust government and institutional claims, viewing the moon landing as a plausible hoax among other hidden truths
Mainstream believers in scientific consensus and established historical facts who accept the moon landing as genuine despite general skepticism toward authorities

Conspiracy-minded individuals who actively believe the moon landing was faked as part of broader patterns of government deception
Skeptics of conspiracy theories who trust mainstream scientific and historical accounts. They consistently reject claims about hidden truths regarding vaccines, moon landings, and the Holocaust.
Cautious moderates who acknowledge some possibility of institutional deception but lean toward accepting official accounts. They tend to pick 'probably false' across conspiracy questions.
Conspiracy-minded individuals who believe powerful groups deliberately hide dangerous truths about health, science, and history. They're skeptical of official narratives across multiple domains.

Skeptics of conspiracy theories who trust mainstream scientific and medical institutions. They believe vaccine safety is well-established and scrutinized by independent bodies.

Conspiracy-minded individuals who believe pharmaceutical companies and governments actively conceal vaccine dangers from the public.
Uncertain respondents without strong convictions on vaccine safety claims or the extent of institutional transparency around them.
Skeptics of official narratives who believe governments engage in major conspiracies; they see 9/11 as part of a pattern of hidden truths about moon landings, vaccines, and other cover-ups.
Mainstream believers in official accounts who trust government institutions and scientific consensus; they reject conspiracy theories across domains including 9/11.

Uncertain moderates who lack strong conviction either way, finding 9/11 claims plausible but not compelling; they reflect the general Italian skepticism toward institutions without committing to specific theories.
Selective skeptics who question some official narratives (particularly on vaccines and health) but remain more conventional on geopolitical events like 9/11.
Skeptics of conspiracy theories who reject Holocaust denial based on historical evidence and ethical conviction that such denialism is harmful and false.
Conspiracy-minded individuals who are receptive to revisionist historical claims and distrust official narratives across multiple domains.
Uncertain respondents who lack strong conviction on this sensitive historical question and prefer to express doubt rather than take a clear position.
Skeptics of official narratives who believe governments routinely deceive the public on major events; influenced by patterns of distrust seen across vaccine and AIDS conspiracy responses.
Mainstream believers in official accounts who accept the 9/11 Commission findings and reject conspiracy theories, similar to those who strongly reject moon landing hoaxes.
Genuinely uncertain individuals who lack strong conviction either way, reflecting the substantial 'Don't know' responses seen across multiple conspiracy questions in this group.
Skeptics of conspiracy theories who trust mainstream scientific and institutional accounts. They reject claims about intentional creation and spread of AIDS.
Conspiracy-minded individuals who believe powerful groups deliberately create and weaponize diseases for population control or other nefarious purposes.
Uncertain moderates who see some plausibility in the claim but lack strong conviction either way, reflecting broader distrust in institutions without full commitment to conspiracy narratives.

Skeptics of US institutions and geopolitical narratives who believe Trump-Russia coordination is plausible given broader patterns of hidden truths; influenced by distrust of official accounts seen in vaccine and 9/11 conspiracy responses.
Mainstream consensus followers who accept the established investigation findings that Trump's team did not knowingly coordinate with Russia, viewing this as settled by official inquiries.
Uncertain pragmatists who lack strong conviction either way, viewing the Trump-Russia question as politically contested rather than factually resolved, similar to their ambivalence on vaccines.
Skeptics of climate change consensus who believe the scientific mainstream on global warming is exaggerated or politically motivated; they see it as a hoax or deception.
Mainstream Canadians who accept the scientific consensus on climate change and reject the hoax narrative, viewing it as well-established fact.
Uncertain middle group who are unsure about the extent of human responsibility for climate change or whether the 'hoax' framing is accurate.
